topic: Patterns and Problems in Emerging Multi-Agent Systems

key_points: Orchestration vs choreography is the design decision nobody names: centralized inspectable workflow logic vs emergent distributed control; default to orchestration until the observability cost of choreography is a deliberate choice.
Four coordination topologies in production: orchestrator-worker (~70% of deployments), sequential pipeline, dynamic handoff (swarm), hierarchical multi-level orchestration.

The canonical production incident: a multi-agent research system ran 11 days at 99.99% uptime, 0.0% error rate, and a $47,000 cloud bill because agents were stuck in an infinite retry loop — wrongness does not show up in Grafana.

Inter-agent bugs are mostly semantic, not transport: a correctly formatted message carrying logically wrong output propagates unchecked. Every handoff needs a typed, validated contract (Pydantic) at the boundary.

Structural failures need structural fixes: circuit breakers per downstream service, saga compensating actions for side-effectful steps, hard retry ceilings in code, durable WorkflowState with checkpoint resume.
Three topologies dominate 2026: supervisor/hierarchical, orchestrator-worker (about 70% of production deployments, incl. Anthropic and OpenAI reference designs), and swarm.
Honest economics: independent multi-agent setups incur ~58% extra token overhead; centralized ones ~285% — multi-agent only pays off on genuine specialization, parallelism, or critique.

Five multi-agent-only failure modes: orchestrator bottleneck, agreement bias in debate (majority pressure suppresses independent correction), observability collapse, token cost explosion, and role drift across long turns.

Mitigations that work: small fast model as router with a circuit breaker on routing oscillation, blind voting with independent first pass before inter-agent visibility, per-task token caps, role-restricted tool sets.
Framework success-rate table (relative ranking, not absolute capability): LangGraph ~62%, AutoGen/AG2 ~58%, CrewAI ~54%; AutoGen is in maintenance mode with AG2 as the community fork.
Six orchestration patterns cover >95% of production scenarios: sequential pipeline, parallel fan-out/fan-in, hierarchical supervisor-worker, swarm, blackboard, hybrid.

MAST trace analysis of 1,642 executions: 41.77% system design issues (step repetition, wrong tool, context overflow, missing termination), 36.94% inter-agent misalignment, 21.30% task verification failures.
Orchestration topology has a larger effect on performance than model choice — AdaptOrch reports 12–23% SWE-bench gains from choosing the right topology.

Four pitfalls: context pollution across handoffs (fix: schema validation + confidence threshold ~0.7), runaway loops/cost explosions (hard caps: max iterations 10, max tool calls 20, max tokens 50k), over-engineering (sweet spot is 3–8 agents), demo-to-production guardrail gap.
Adopt MCP (tool access) + A2A (inter-agent delegation) on new projects to avoid a costly later migration.

Four canonical topologies — solo, supervisor (hub-and-spoke), mesh (peer-to-peer), hierarchical — with an explicit escalation rule: start solo, move to supervisor only when one agent cannot cover the breadth.
The single most common architectural mistake in 2026 is over-decomposing: 8–12 agents where 3–4 produce the same quality at one-third the coordination overhead.

Seven coordination patterns that work: routing with confidence scores, plan-then-execute with verification, parallel exploration with selection, sequential refinement, reflection/critique loop, stop-the-line, tool-use-first-then-synthesis.

Three memory levels (short-term intra-agent, long-term persistent, shared inter-agent) with anti-patterns: context overflow, no invalidation/TTL, unstructured shared memory, memory pollution from one bad run.
Production failure modes to design against: agent timeout, tool failure, malformed model output, plan failure, coordination deadlock, resource exhaustion, quality failure, cascade failure.
The canonical pattern that emerged in late 2025 is the Orchestrator-Worker-Critic triad: orchestrator decomposes and routes, specialized workers execute, a critic reviews and triggers retries.

What works in production: narrow agents beat general ones; deterministic (hard-coded) handoffs beat LLM-routed handoffs; critic loops are not optional (systems without a review step run 3–5x higher error rates).
Memory is still the unsolved problem — every team has a different shared-memory solution (Qdrant, Mem0, custom Redis schemas) and none are satisfied; consolidation is expected.
The emerging successor to fixed hierarchies is the agent mesh: peer networks with capability manifests and a registry routing each subtask to the best available agent.
Mesh observability is the hard part — a single request fans out into hundreds of agent-to-agent calls, so every call must be tagged, logged, and counted.
MAST (Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?) is the first empirically grounded MAS failure taxonomy: 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 popular frameworks, kappa 0.88 inter-annotator agreement.
14 fine-grained failure modes clustered into three categories: (i) specification and system design, (ii) inter-agent misalignment, (iii) task verification and termination.

Performance gains from multi-agent coordination over single-agent baselines are frequently minimal; specification/design issues and inter-agent misalignment account for the substantial majority of observed failures (~42% and ~37%).
Failure distribution is framework-specific: AppWorld suffers premature termination, OpenManus step repetition, HyperAgent step repetition plus incorrect verification.

The two proposed cheap interventions — better role specification and better orchestration — did not fix the identified failures; structural interventions such as improved inter-agent social reasoning are required.
Academic empirical anchor: 7 MAS frameworks, 200+ tasks, 6 expert annotators, 1K+ annotated traces, inter-annotator Cohen's Kappa 0.88.
14 failure modes in 3 categories: FC1 specification/system-design issues, FC2 inter-agent misalignment, FC3 task verification & termination.
Failure distribution is balanced rather than dominated by one category (FC1 41.77%, FC2 36.94%, FC3 21.30%) — failures are diverse, not one fix away.

Most common individual modes: reasoning-action mismatch 13.98%, fail to ask for clarification 11.65%, premature termination 7.82%, task derailment 7.15%, no/incomplete verification 6.82%, incorrect verification 6.66%.
SOTA open-source MAS correctness can be as low as 25% (ChatDev); MAS gains over single-agent or best-of-N baselines are often minimal.

Prompt/orchestration interventions help but are insufficient: role-specification improvements gave ~+9.4% success on ChatDev (GPT-4o). Conclusion: MAS design needs organizational understanding, not just stronger base models.

Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems runs 180 controlled configurations (SAS plus Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid MAS across OpenAI/Google/Anthropic model tiers) to isolate architecture from model choice.
Measured coordination overhead relative to a single-agent baseline: independent 58%, centralized 285%, decentralized 263%, hybrid 515%.
Topology-dependent error amplification: independent agents amplify errors 17.2x through unchecked propagation, while centralized coordination contains this to 4.4x.

Results span +81% relative improvement (structured financial reasoning, centralized) to -70% degradation (sequential planning, independent): architecture-task alignment, not agent count, determines success.

A capability ceiling exists — coordination yields diminishing and then negative returns once single-agent baselines exceed roughly 45%; tool-heavy tasks suffer disproportionately because coordination fragments the per-agent token budget.

Anthropic's production Research feature: Lead Researcher plans and spawns parallel subagents with separate context windows that compress findings back to the lead — the canonical orchestrator-worker reference design.

Three factors explained 95% of BrowseComp performance variance; token usage alone explained 80%, with tool-call count and model choice as the rest — multi-agent works largely because it spends enough tokens.
Multi-agent with Opus 4 lead and Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on breadth-first research.
Cost reality: agents use ~4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems ~15x — economic viability requires high-value tasks.

Poor fit cases stated plainly: domains needing shared context across all agents and tightly interdependent work such as most coding tasks; also note the 2025 'Building Effective Agents' guidance to start with the simplest composable pattern.
The production-counterpart article: orchestrator + parallel subagents, and the strongest quantitative ROI figures in the space.
Multi-agent (Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval; the win is concentrated on breadth-first, parallelizable queries.
Cost accounting: agents use ~4x more tokens than chat; multi-agent systems ~15x; token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance.
Engineering lessons: error compounding in stateful long-running agents; resume-from-failure instead of restart; rainbow deployments; full production tracing; end-state (not turn-by-turn) evaluation.
Anti-pattern: synchronous subagent execution blocks the lead agent from steering, subagents from coordinating, and stalls the whole system on one slow subagent.
Prompt/tool design matters more than framework choice; heuristics beat rigid rules; source-quality heuristics were needed to stop agents preferring SEO content farms.
Production multi-agent LLM systems fail at rates between 41% and 87%, with the majority of failures attributable to coordination defects rather than base-model capability.

79% of observed failures originate from specification and coordination issues — reinforced by production analyses of semantic intent divergence, where cooperating agents develop inconsistent interpretations of the same objective.
Argues coordination should be a first-class, separable architectural layer distinct from the information layer and the per-agent logic layer.

Semantic drift is a first-class failure mode: in LLM coordination, messages drift in meaning across rounds even when no single step looks wrong — a continuous failure with no analogue in classical coordination.

competitors.title: Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems (Anthropic Frontier Red Team, Aug 13 2026)
key_points: Primary source for the topic; the post title is effectively the keyword. Anchored HN discussion (200 points, 138 comments).

Defines the core distinction: agents work well when they treat each other as tool invocations (prompts in, artifacts out) and stumble when they must treat each other as distinct, long-lived peers with no clear hierarchy.

45-agent coordinated swarm on 15 OSS repos found 266 vulnerabilities vs 21 for independent parallel agents (21 over 6.5M tokens; 266 over 27M); only 12 vulnerabilities in common, so the two methods are complementary.

Software-engineering swarms (12h fantasy-game task) largely failed to merge work; baseline, prescriptive-roles and 'CEO hierarchy' prompts made little difference to the outcome. Coordination style differed sharply by model generation.
Failure families with evidence: conformity/low variance, epistemic gullibility and consensus bias, and incompatible goals escalating into 'turf war' sabotage.
Conclusion: coordination does not emerge automatically from stronger intelligence or individual-level alignment; it needs environment/mechanism design.

competitors.title: Don't Build Multi-Agents (Cognition / Devin, Jun 12 2025)
key_points: The strongest counter-position and the best source of the design principles that decide when multi-agent is safe.
Principle 1: share context — share full agent traces, not just individual messages.
Principle 2: actions carry implicit decisions, so conflicting decisions produce bad results (two subagents built an inconsistent game asset and background from the same request).
Argues parallel subagents are fragile in 2025 because cross-agent context passing is unsolved; recommends single-threaded linear agents plus a dedicated context-compression model.
Notes Claude Code's deliberately conservative subagent design (sequential, question-answering only, no concurrent parallel writers) as the safe pattern.

competitors.title: Building Effective Agents (Anthropic Engineering)
key_points: Canonical pattern catalogue that most 'multi-agent design patterns' guides derive from: augmented LLM building block, then prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning vs voting), orchestrator-workers, and autonomous agents.
Key framing: prefer the simplest composable pattern that solves the problem; workflow patterns are for decomposable/known paths, agents for open-ended paths.
Orchestrator-workers vs parallelization: the difference is flexibility — subtasks are determined dynamically by the orchestrator, not pre-defined.
Voting/sectioning rationale: separate focused LLM calls outperform one call handling multiple considerations.

competitors.title: Magentic-One: A Generalist Multi-Agent System (Microsoft Research, arXiv 2411.04468)
key_points: Reference production-grade generalist architecture: one Orchestrator lead agent plus specialized agents (web browser, file navigation, Python coder).
Explicit anti-stall machinery: an outer loop holding a task ledger (facts, facts to look up, facts to derive, educated guesses) and an inner loop holding a progress ledger.

Inner loop answers five questions each iteration: task complete? looping? forward progress? who speaks next? what instruction? A stuck counter (threshold <= 2) triggers re-planning and context resets.
Modular, additive design: agents can be added/removed without prompt retuning, which is the practical argument for role-specialized agents.
Ships AutoGenBench for isolated, repeatable agentic evaluation because agent actions have side effects.

stats.fact: Centralized (orchestrator/supervisor) multi-agent architectures incur about 285% coordination overhead in token cost versus a tuned single-agent baseline; independent peer setups ~58%, decentralized ~263%, hybrid ~515%.
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.08296v3 (Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems)

stats.fact: Independent multi-agent coordination amplifies errors 17.2x through unchecked propagation, while centralized coordination with a validation bottleneck contains amplification to 4.4x.

Multi-agent systems use roughly 15x more tokens than chat interactions (single agents ~4x), and token usage alone explains 80% of the performance variance on BrowseComp (95% with tool-call count and model choice).
An Opus-4-led system with Sonnet-4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on breadth-first research tasks.

MAST analyzed 1,600+ execution traces across 7 MAS frameworks and identified 14 failure modes in 3 categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification/termination) at kappa=0.88 annotator agreement.
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657 (Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?)

stats.fact: Failure distribution in 1,642 analyzed traces: 41.77% system design issues, 36.94% inter-agent misalignment, 21.30% task verification failures.
79% of multi-agent failures originate from specification and coordination issues rather than base-model limitations; production multi-agent LLM systems fail at rates between 41% and 87%.
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03310 (Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems)

stats.fact: Orchestration topology has a larger effect on performance than underlying model choice, delivering 12-23% gains on benchmarks such as SWE-bench when the right topology is selected.
Orchestrator-worker is roughly 70% of production multi-agent deployments in 2026, including most internal builds at Stripe and Mercury and the public Anthropic/OpenAI reference designs.
Reported token duplication rates reach 86% in flat multi-agent topologies and 72% in linear topologies, making redundant artifact retransmission rather than generation the dominant cost driver.
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.15183v1 (Token Coherence: Adapting MESI Cache Protocols)

stats.fact: A supervised multi-agent efficiency layer (SupervisorAgent, ICLR 2026) cut GAIA token consumption by an average of 29.68% with competitive success rates, at a supervisor overhead of only 15.45% of total tokens.
Systems without a critic/review step show 3-5x higher error rates in production; the practical production sweet spot is 3-8 agents, and teams commonly over-decompose into 8-12 agents.
A production research system ran for 11 days with 99.99% uptime, 0.0% error rate and green dashboards while stuck in an infinite retry loop that produced a $47,000 cloud bill.

Failure-aware observability over 165 GAIA traces: 22/53 level-1, 33/86 level-2 and 12/26 level-3 runs failed to produce a usable final answer, with mean token use rising from 8,152 (level 1) to 16,389 (level 3).
stats.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.01365v1 (Early Diagnosis of Wasted Computation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems)

stats.fact: Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol reached 50+ partners and v1.0 in early 2026 with over 100 enterprise organizations, while Anthropic's Model Context Protocol passed 97 million monthly SDK downloads.
AdaptOrch-style case evidence: Google's internal Agent Bake-Off reported a distributed multi-agent architecture cutting processing time from one hour to ten minutes (6x).

A multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead + Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval; gains concentrate on breadth-first, parallelizable queries.
Agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems about 15x more than chats — the core economic constraint on multi-agent architecture.
Three factors explained 95% of performance variance on the BrowseComp evaluation; token usage alone explained 80%, with tool-call count and model choice as the other two.
Parallelization (lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel; subagents use 3+ tools in parallel) cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

A coordinated swarm of 45 agents (each on its own VM with a shared forum) found 266 vulnerabilities across 15 open-source projects, versus 21 for fully independent parallel agents; 21 came from a 6.5M-token run, 266 from a 27M-token run, and only 12 vulnerabilities were common to both methods.
18 of 30 agents on the same model, started simultaneously, created a git branch with the identical name 'mvp-game-loop' — evidence of low-variance, correlated agent behavior.
In a finite-bandwidth job-queue experiment with no coordination mechanism, agents flooded the system with 30Hz polling daemons: 2.4 million job requests were made and only 117 jobs were accepted.

In a Bertrand pricing game with 3-8 agents, agents agreed on explicit price floors by round 3 when given a private back-channel — and still price-matched to the penny via a public listings board after all direct communication channels were removed.

On hidden-profile tasks (where decisive evidence is privately held and group discussion must surface it), the best model's groups scored about 85% while other models' groups scored 17-36%, versus solo ceilings near 100% — deliberation does not saturate with model intelligence.
MAST was derived from 7 popular MAS frameworks, 200+ tasks and 6 expert annotators, yielding 14 failure modes in 3 categories at Cohen's Kappa 0.88 (0.77-0.79 for the LLM-as-judge annotator).

MAS failure distribution is balanced across categories (FC1 specification 41.77%, FC2 inter-agent misalignment 36.94%, FC3 task verification 21.30%), and the strongest single modes are reasoning-action mismatch (13.98%), fail to ask for clarification (11.65%) and premature termination (7.82%).
The correctness of the SOTA open-source MAS ChatDev can be as low as 25%; prompt and topology interventions improved ChatDev by roughly +9.4% (GPT-4o) but did not resolve most failures.

Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls, and estimates only about 130 of thousands of self-described agentic AI vendors are real ('agent washing').
Gartner expects agents in use per company to grow from about 15 in 2025 to as many as 150,000 per company by 2028.

A2A (Agent2Agent) was released by Google in April 2025, moved to Linux Foundation governance in June 2025, reached v1.0 in 2026, and absorbed IBM's ACP in August 2025; it is the agent-to-agent complement to MCP, which connects agents to tools.

Enterprise data cited in a 2026 context-engineering paper: 75% of enterprises plan agentic AI deployment within two years, while deployment has surged and retreated as organizations hit scaling complexity.

angles: Start negative: the strongest production heuristic in 2026 is NOT to build multi-agent. Lead with the capability ceiling (~45% single-agent baseline), shared-context and interdependence no-fits, and the tuned-single-agent ceiling check before any topology is chosen.

Coordination, not intelligence, is the failure surface: ~79% of failures are specification/coordination defects and production failure rates run 41-87%. Frame the whole guide around coordination as a separable architectural layer.

The uncomfortable token economics: multi-agent works largely because it spends enough tokens (80% of BrowseComp variance), at 15x chat token cost and up to 515% coordination overhead. Pair every pattern with its cost signature.
Topology beats model choice (12-23% benchmark gains) — so the guide's central artifact is a topology/pattern selection decision tree, not a framework leaderboard.

Failure taxonomy as a debugging instrument: MAST's 14 modes across 3 categories, plus semantic drift and error amplification (17.2x independent vs 4.4x centralized), give readers a checklist for auditing their own system.

Wrong-but-green: the $47,000 infinite-loop incident plus MAST trace evidence show standard service monitoring (latency/error/uptime) is blind to application-layer wrongness — observability must be designed first.

Structural fixes only: prompt tweaks do not fix structural failures. Cover typed Pydantic handoff contracts, circuit breakers per downstream dependency, saga compensation for side-effectful steps, hard retry/token caps, and durable checkpointed WorkflowState.

Interoperability shift: MCP for agent-to-tool and A2A for agent-to-agent is now the dual protocol stack, making cross-vendor orchestration (LangGraph orchestrator + ADK worker + CrewAI crew) a real 2026 pattern.

Lead with the primary source: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team post literally titled 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems' — it is the discourse anchor (HN 200 points / 138 comments) and its framing ('agents as tools vs agents as peers') is the cleanest organizing idea for the whole guide.

The conformity / low-variance failure mode is the most under-covered insight in competing guides: because agents are low-variance, one bad decision replicates system-wide, turning isolated errors into systemic failure. Tie it to the branch-name, raytracer and Bertrand collusion evidence.

Give readers the two-sided debate rather than one camp: Anthropic's 90.2% research win vs Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents'. The resolution is specifiability — multi-agent pays off when subtasks are parallelizable and share no implicit decisions, and collapses when they do.

Cost as the gating design decision: the 15x token multiplier (and 4x for a single agent) converts 'should we use multi-agent?' into an explicit ROI question rather than an architecture preference. Pair it with Gartner's >40% cancellation prediction to show the failure is economic as often as technical.

Turn the MAST taxonomy into an operational asset: map each of the 14 failure modes to a concrete control (termination criteria, clarification permissions, verifier independence, artifact handoff) so the guide is actionable rather than descriptive.

Context engineering is the real lever: context isolation, full-trace sharing, and end-state evaluation. Cite the five context-quality criteria (relevance, sufficiency, isolation, economy, provenance) as the checklist.
Anti-stall machinery as a named pattern: Magentic-One's task ledger / progress ledger with a stuck counter is a portable design that most 'patterns' guides omit entirely.

Observability is a first-class requirement: agents fail silently (bad decisions, infinite tool loops, polite refusals) rather than crashing, so trace-level debugging and end-state evaluation are non-negotiable before scaling agent counts.
